item.title: Limbic circuit alterations in bipolar disorder.
item.description:
Dialogues in clinical neuroscience
INTRODUCTION: This study investigated the spatial and temporal pattern of brain white matter (WM) alterations and their relationship with intrinsic brain activity in bipolar disorder (BD). METHODS: Multimodal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) data were collected from 67 BD patients (during manic, depressive, or euthymic phases) and 125 healthy controls (HC) at baseline, and from a subsample of 33 BD patients (in a different illness phase) and 23 HC after follow-up. Analyses of diffusion MRI and resting-state functional MRI were performed to characterise fixel-based metrics in WM and their relationship with intrinsic brain activity in BD and HC, as well as across timepoints. RESULTS: BD exhibited a spatial pattern of WM alterations characterised by reductions in fibre density and/or bundle cross-section involving fornix and cingulum (major limbic pathways), alongside portions of other tracts, compared with HC. Reduced fibre density in the fornix was associated with intrinsic activity changes involving midbrain, thalamus, and connected fronto-temporal cortical areas within the default-mode network in BD. These alterations showed no significant changes over time or across illness phases. CONCLUSIONS: These findings converge on limbic circuit alterations and suggest a relationship between structural abnormalities of the fornix and functional changes in intrinsic brain architecture in BD.

item.title: Excitation/Inhibition Balance in People at Clinical High Risk for Psychosis: A Functional MRI Study
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Excitation/inhibition (E/I) imbalance is implicated in the pathophysiology of psychosis, but the extent to which this is evident before the onset of illness is unclear. Here, we investigated E/I-related brain dynamics using the Hurst exponent (HE) derived from resting-state MRI in two longitudinal cohorts of individuals at clinical high risk for psychosis (CHR-P): PSYSCAN (190 CHR-P individuals and 115 controls) and Accelerating Medicines Partnership® Schizophrenia (826 CHR-P individuals and 241 controls). Both cohorts showed lower whole-brain HE in CHR-P individuals than in controls at baseline, with the most prominent differences observed in the somatomotor network and thalamus. In both cohorts, normative receptor distributions significantly predicted the spatial pattern of HE differences, with consistent contributions from norepinephrine, serotonin, and opioid receptors. In PSYSCAN, 21 CHR-P individuals transitioned to psychosis during follow-up. There was preliminary evidence that subsequent transition to psychosis was associated with a longitudinal reduction in HE in the right inferior parietal cortex and that baseline regional HE showed above-chance prediction of subsequent transition at the individual level. Together, these findings suggest that vulnerability to psychosis is associated with reduced HE, consistent with less persistent brain dynamics and increased excitability.

item.title: Connectomic Flow Across Cortical Sensory Systems in Juvenile Fibromyalgia
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Adult fibromyalgia (FM) is characterized by altered functional connectivity between sensory, salience, and default mode networks (DMN), yet its early emergence and hierarchical organization remain unclear in Juvenile Fibromyalgia (JFM). We used stepwise functional connectivity (SFC) to detect early changes in the hierarchical integration of sensory signals toward salience and heteromodal networks in adolescents with JFM. Additionally, we assessed whether these alterations overlap with FM-associated gene expression from the Allen Human Brain Atlas (AHBA). Forty-six adolescent females with JFM (16.44-1.11 years) and forty-three healthy females (16.09-1.06 years) completed clinical questionnaires and underwent resting-state fMRI. Whole-brain voxel-wise SFC mapped connectivity patterns from primary sensory regions (visual, somatosensory, auditory) toward the DMN across increasing link-step distances. Regression models examined associations between symptom severity and SFC measures. Spatial overlap between functional findings and FM-associated gene expression profiles was also evaluated. Both groups showed a similar pattern, progressing from primary to secondary sensory regions, then to multimodal integration and salience areas, and finally to heteromodal DMN cortices. Greater symptom severity was associated with reduced second-step connectivity between secondary somatosensory cortices and the right anterior insula/operculum (T=5.11, pFWE<0.05). The neuronal transcription factor MYT1L showed relatively higher expression in AHBA in an overlapping region including the pars opercularis. Large-scale sensory-to-heteromodal functional architecture appears preserved in JFM. However, patients with greater symptom burden show reduced propagation of somatosensory information toward salience-interoceptive regions, suggesting altered multimodal processing. This disruption spatially overlaps with MYT1L expression, pointing towards a developmentally sensitive circuit vulnerability in severe patients.

item.title: Quantitative Resting-State Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging Reveals White Matter Network Reorganization in Older Adults With White Matter Hyperintensities
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Background/Objectives: White matter hyperintensities (WMH) are important imaging markers of cerebral small vessel disease in older adults and are closely associated with cognitive decline. However, WMH burden alone cannot fully explain interindividual differences in cognitive impairment. This study constructed white matter resting-state functional networks based on the multimodal white matter atlas (MWMA) and investigated WMH-related alterations in network topology and their associations with cognitive function. Methods This single-center cross-sectional study included 171 older adults, comprising 50 participants with absent or mild white matter hyperintensities and 121 participants with moderate-to-severe white matter hyperintensities. All participants underwent three-dimensional T1-weighted imaging, T2-FLAIR imaging, and resting-state BOLD-fMRI. WMH grading and segmentation were performed using T2-FLAIR images. White matter network nodes were defined using the MWMA atlas, and 173 cerebral white matter regions of interest were retained. Individual 173 × 173 white matter functional connectivity matrices were constructed. Graph-theoretical metrics were calculated across a sparsity range of 0.05–0.50, and area under the curve values were used for statistical analysis. Group differences were assessed using general linear models adjusted for age, sex, years of education, and mean framewise displacement. Exploratory partial correlation analyses were performed in participants with complete cognitive data. Results Both groups retained small-world organization. Compared with controls, the WMH group showed increased aγ and aσ, whereas aEglob, aEloc, and aLp did not differ significantly. The WMH group also showed increased DMN-SMN inter-module connectivity, without significant intra-module differences. Nodal abnormalities were spatially heterogeneous: increased aBc was mainly located in WMH-affected regions, whereas abnormal aDc and aNe were more often distributed in normal-appearing white matter. Several abnormal nodal metrics were associated with TMT-A, TMT-B, and MoCA performance. Conclusions Moderate-to-severe WMH is associated with white matter functional network reorganization rather than complete topological breakdown. These alterations may contribute to WMH-related cognitive decline, particularly impairments in processing speed and executive function.

item.title: Structural and resting-state functional brain alterations in male smokers: a combined voxel-based morphometry and functional connectivity analysis.
item.description:
Nicotine & tobacco research : official journal of the Society for Research on Nicotine and Tobacco
Introduction Neuroimaging studies have demonstrated that chronic smoking is associated with gray matter volume (GMV) reductions and resting-state functional connectivity (rsFC) abnormalities. However, these changes have largely been investigated independently, and the relationship between regional GMV alterations and corresponding rsFC changes remains poorly characterized. Integrating structural and functional metrics may enhance understanding of the neural mechanisms underlying nicotine dependence. Methods We recruited 51 male smokers and 52 age-matched healthy controls. Voxel-based morphometry (VBM) was performed to identify regions with significant GMV differences between groups. These regions were subsequently used as seeds for seed-based whole-brain rsFC analysis. Results Compared with controls, smokers exhibited significantly reduced GMV in the bilateral fusiform gyrus, left temporal pole (TP), and right inferior occipital gyrus. Smokers also showed enhanced rsFC within multiple circuits, including the left fusiform gyrus-right TP, left TP-left inferior frontal gyrus, and right fusiform gyrus-left rolandic operculum, whereas rsFC between the right fusiform gyrus and left insula was significantly decreased. Correlation analyses revealed that left TP GMV was negatively correlated with smoking duration and cumulative tobacco exposure (pack-years). Furthermore, rsFC strength between the left fusiform gyrus and right TP was negatively correlated with both the Fagerström Test for Nicotine Dependence (FTND) and DSM-5 tobacco use disorder severity scores. Conclusions These findings suggest that chronic smoking is associated with concurrent GMV reductions and rsFC alterations within visual, social cognitive, and sensorimotor networks, with the left fusiform gyrus-right TP connectivity showing potential relevance to the severity of tobacco use disorder.

item.title: Resting-State Alpha Power and Cross-Hemispheric Beta Connectivity Are Associated With Individual Differences in Voice Identity Perception.
item.description:
Journal of speech, language, and hearing research : JSLHR
Purpose Human voices convey not only linguistic content but also rich information about speaker identity. Individual differences in voice discrimination are robust and trait-like, yet their neurophysiological substrates remain unclear. In the present study, we investigated whether resting-state electroencephalography (rsEEG) is associated with individual differences in voice identity perception, assessed using the Sisu Voice Matching Test (SVMT). Method A total of 61 native Mandarin speakers underwent eyes-open and eyes-closed rsEEG recordings, from which spectral power and interchannel coherence were extracted across eight canonical frequency bands. Behavioral performance on SVMT was examined alongside additional cognitive and perceptual measures, and principal component analysis was used to derive orthogonal covariates for specificity analyses, which enabled us to determine whether the rsEEG-SVMT relationships were independent of broader cognitive factors. Results Our results revealed distinct neural-behavioral associations across resting-state conditions: In eyes-open recordings, alpha-band power was positively associated with accuracy on telling-together trials, while cross-hemispheric beta-band coherence between right frontal and left temporo-parietal regions correlated with overall and pseudo-word performance. In contrast, eyes-closed spectral power showed limited explanatory value, with a specific negative beta coherence between left central and right posterior sites associated with poorer performance. Notably, the alpha power effect was attenuated after controlling for domain-general cognitive factors, whereas the beta coherence-SVMT associations remained robust, indicating greater specificity to voice identity processing. Conclusions These findings suggest that individual differences in voice discrimination are grounded in stable neural traits that are differentially expressed across background resting-state conditions. Specifically, they support a two-tier framework in which spectral power reflects domain-general cognitive readiness, whereas network-level beta-band connectivity constitutes a more selective neural signature of voice identity perception. Supplemental material https://doi.org/10.23641/asha.34914567.

item.title: Insomnia reorganizes large-scale functional connectivity abnormalities in depression: Evidence from functional gradients and neurotransmitter mapping.
item.description:
NeuroImage
Sleep disorders are one of the most prevalent and clinically important features of depression, yet their impact on the large-scale organization of brain functional abnormalities remains unclear. Here, we investigated whether insomnia reshapes whole-brain resting-state functional connectivity (RSFC) abnormalities in depression and alter their hierarchical and neurochemical organization. Resting-state fMRI data were acquired from depressed patients with (INS, n = 32) and without insomnia symptoms (NINS, n = 24), and healthy controls (HC, n = 45). Network-based statistics (NBS) was used to identify altered RSFC subnetworks. We then examined the hierarchical distribution of network abnormalities using the principal functional gradient, assessed clinical relevance, and evaluated their spatial correspondence with neurotransmitter atlas. Results showed that the INS group exhibited more widespread functional connectivity impairments, primarily concentrated in the visual and sensorimotor networks. Moreover, these abnormal connections showed a hierarchical distribution pattern along the principal functional gradient, with lower-level sensory systems more affected than higher-level cognitive networks. Significant differences in node degree were observed in the visual network, and functional connectivity within this network was associated with anxiety scores in the INS group. Spatial similarity analyses revealed overlapping but distinct neurotransmitter profiles across groups, with shared correlations for mGluR5 and stronger μ-opioid-related associations in the INS group. These findings suggest that insomnia symptoms in depression are associated not simply with more severe dysfunction, but with a reorganization of large-scale functional abnormalities toward lower-order sensory systems, characterized by a gradient-dependent connectivity distribution and altered associations with specific neurotransmitter systems, particularly μ-opioid receptors.

item.title: Altered frontoparietal BOLD-CSF coupling in drug-naïve young adults with major depressive disorder: Links to neural variability, cognition, and GABAergic gene expression.
item.description:
Journal of affective disorders
Glymphatic dysfunction, indexed non-invasively via BOLD-CSF coupling, a putative proxy for cerebrospinal fluid clearance, has been implicated in mood disorders, but its regional relationships with neural activity, network dynamics, cognition, and molecular features in major depressive disorder (MDD) remain unclear. We analyzed resting-state fMRI from 109 MDD patients and 106 healthy controls (HC), assessing BOLD-CSF coupling at global, network, and subnetwork levels and its associations with mfALFF, BOLD signal variability (SDBOLD), functional connectivity (FC), cognition, and Allen Human Brain Atlas transcriptomic profiles. MDD patients showed modestly reduced global BOLD-CSF coupling (p = 0.036), concentrated in higher-order networks (p = 0.013), including the default mode and frontoparietal networks (FPN, both p = 0.019). Coupling was negatively correlated with SDBOLD and FC across most networks (q < 0.05), and the coupling-FC relationship was selectively weaker within the FPN in MDD (q = 0.019), supported by a group-by-coupling interaction. Within the FPN, SDBOLD was associated with cognitive performance, and mediation analysis indicated an indirect pathway from FPN coupling to cognition via SDBOLD that was nominally significant in HC but not MDD, although the moderating effect of group was not itself significant. Transcriptomic analysis linked regional coupling alterations to gene expression (30.3% variance explained, p = 0.040) enriched for GABAergic signaling. These findings suggest that BOLD-CSF coupling alterations in MDD, concentrated in higher-order networks, are associated with altered neural variability, disrupted connectivity, and cognitive deficits, and spatially correspond with the cortical expression of genes enriched for receptor and channel functions.

item.title: A dynamical mechanism for opposing cortical gradients in resting-state functional and stimulation-derived effective connectomes
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Resting-state functional connectivity (FC) and stimulation-derived effective connectivity (EC) offer complementary views of cortical interactions, yet how cortical dynamics shape their relationship within a shared anatomical network remains unclear. Using group-level resting-state fMRI and intracranial electrical stimulation data from large-scale human cohorts, we find that regional mean response to electrical stimulation is negatively correlated with its mean FC (r=-0.568), with the two measures exhibiting opposing trends along the cortical hierarchy. To account for this divergence, we develop a differentiable whole-cortex mean-field model with independently trainable regional parameters, fitted to EC and FC through two-stage EC--FC training using gradient-based optimization. The optimized model reproduces EC (r=0.733) and FC (r=0.726) connectomes and their opposing regional signatures. Without prescribing a hierarchical parameter map, training yields a consistent organization in which recurrent strength and intrinsic noise increase from sensory to association cortex, whereas background input decreases. Linearization based analytical argument and parameter perturbation experiments further suggest how this organization can enhance evoked responsiveness while weakening resting-state correlations along the cortical hierarchy. Together, these findings link opposing connectome signatures, cortical hierarchy and emergent regional parameter organization, while providing a deep-learning-enabled, multimodal modelling framework for investigating cortical dynamics.

item.title: Evidence supporting resting-state power spectrum exponent as a non-invasive measure of neural-circuit excitation:inhibition balance in children with and without autism
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Introduction: An ongoing neural circuit excitation (E) and inhibition (I) imbalance is thought to be a major contributor to clinical conditions such as autism, schizophrenia, and epilepsy. Current methods for directly measuring E:I dynamics require invasive procedures that are difficult to perform in non-human animals and nearly impossible in humans. A non-invasive measure of E:I balance is of great interest as a diagnostic as well as therapeutic marker, and as a means of studying relevant pathological and intervention mechanisms. Scientists have recently developed a computational model to show that, using resting-state (RS) MEG or EEG recordings, the E:I balance can be estimated from the power law exponent (slope) of the electrophysiological power spectrum. In their model, the RS power spectrum exponent is hypothesized to reflect the integration of synaptic currents in the brain, an index of E:I balance driven largely by excitatory (glutamate, Glu) and inhibitory (gamma-aminobutyric acid, GABA) neurotransmitter levels. Glu and GABA are the principal excitatory and inhibitory neurotransmitters in the brain, together shaping the balance between neural circuit excitation and inhibition. The present study shows that parietal-occipital neurochemistry as a predictor of the parietal-occipital RS exponent is driven by inhibitory neurotransmitter levels in typically developing (TD) children but not in children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD). Methods: Midline parietal-occipital RS power spectra (MEG) and Glu and GABA+ concentration (MRS) were obtained from 129 children (TD N = 84, ASD N = 45) 10.2 to 17.9 years old, with follow-up measures in a subset of the children providing 148 MEG and MRS datasets. Analyses focused on RS neural function and Glu and GABA+ concentration in parietal-occipital cortex. Results: t-tests showed no group differences between the parietal-occipital exponent, Glu, GABA+, or Glu/GABA+ ratio measures (ps > 0.21). In the full sample, older age was marginally associated with a lower exponent (p = 0.07), and older age associated with lower Glu concentration (p < 0.05). Age and GABA concentration or Glu/GABA+ associations were not observed (p > 0.05). There was no main effect of Glu or a Glu x group interaction with the exponent (ps > 0.14). Simple effect analyses of interactions for GABA+ (p < 0.05) and ratio (p<0.05) showed a GABA+ and exponent association for TD (p = 0.01) but not ASD (p = 0.40) and a ratio and exponent association for TD (p = 0.01) but not ASD (p = 0.83). Discussion: The brain chemistry and RS exponent associations suggest that a simple method for estimating E:I ratio reduces a major hurdle in understanding a currently difficult-to-measure, yet fundamental aspect of neural computation that has been proposed as central to clinical conditions such as ASD, epilepsy, and schizophrenia. Present findings indicate that the contribution of local brain chemistry to neural-circuit E:I balance differs for older children with and without ASD, with GABA inhibition presenting the more promising contributor to the E:I balance in TD children. Findings have the potential for high impact, including identifying neural markers for use in tracking treatment response

item.title: Age and bilingual language experience are associated with large-scale functional network reorganization
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
Aging is associated with changes in large-scale functional brain organization, such as reductions in network segregation, which have been interpreted as a feature of age-related neural dedifferentiation. However, functional network organization may may also reflect accumulated life experiences. Bilingualism, in particular, has been linked to experience-dependent variation in cognitive and neural systems supporting language processing and executive control. Whether bilingualism is associated with network segregation across adulthood, and how these associations vary with language experience, remains unclear. To address this question, the present multisite study examines resting-state functional connectivity (RSFC) among the Language network, the Default Mode (DMN), and the Multiple Demand (MD) (which support language processing, internally directed cognition, and domain-general cognitive control, respectively). The sample comprised N= 605 adults spanning younger to older adulthood, drawn from eight independent datasets across four sociolinguistic contexts. Older age was associated with less segregation across all three network pairs. Notably, bilingual adults showed greater Language–DMN, Language–MD, and DMN–MD segregation than monolingual adults. Immersion-defined contrasts further revealed variation across linguistic environments such that both immersed and non-immersed bilinguals showed greater DMN-MD segregation than monolinguals, while greater Language–MD segregation was observed primarily in immersed bilinguals compared to monolinguals. In contrast, continuous measures of bilingual experience were not significantly associated with segregation and did not modulate age-related differences. Together, these findings highlight age-related reductions in network segregation and demonstrate that bilingual language experience is associated with systemic differences in large-scale functional network organization across adulthood.

item.title: Brain Responses to Naturalistic Language During Movie-Watching as Markers of Current and Future Cognitive Function in Older Adults.
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
Monitoring global cognitive function in older adults is crucial for timely detection and intervention of cognitive impairment. While cognitive tests and traditional magnetic resonance imaging have been widely used, more sensitive methods are needed. Conventionally, language production rather than comprehension has been emphasized for monitoring cognitive decline, as comprehension appears preserved in controlled laboratory paradigms. However, naturalistic language comprehension engages multiple aging-sensitive cognitive systems, making language-related brain activations during naturalistic tasks potentially sensitive markers of global cognitive function. This study investigated whether language-related activations during naturalistic movie-watching functional magnetic resonance imaging (mw-fMRI) could effectively monitor older adults' global cognitive function as assessed by the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA). We recruited 97 (43 females and 54 males) non-demented participants aged 60 years or older to undergo MRI scans and complete the MoCA at baseline; 50 (28 females and 22 males) completed follow-up assessments after two years. Language comprehension during movie watching elicited activations in core frontotemporal and extended language networks that significantly correlated with MoCA scores. Using nested cross-validation, support vector classifiers demonstrated that mw-fMRI activation features effectively classified baseline cognitive status (area under the curve [AUC] = 0.811 ± 0.019) and forecasted two-year cognitive change (AUC = 0.763 ± 0.036), outperforming demographics and traditional MRI features. We localized predictive activations and discussed potential compensatory mechanisms underlying these patterns. Our findings highlight naturalistic language comprehension during mw-fMRI as a biologically interpretable, ecologically valid tool for monitoring global cognitive function in older adults.Significance Statement Detection of cognitive decline in older adults is critical for timely intervention, yet current methods have limitations. Conventional laboratory language tasks suggest comprehension remains intact with aging, leading researchers to focus on language production for monitoring decline. However, real-world language comprehension (e.g., understanding conversations in movies) requires coordinating multiple cognitive processes that are vulnerable to aging. We find that brain activations during naturalistic movie watching effectively detect current cognitive status and forecast future cognitive changes, outperforming traditional brain imaging approaches. This passive, engaging task requires no explicit responses, making it feasible for older adults and clinical populations. Our findings establish ecologically valid neural markers that could help identify individuals at risk for cognitive impairment before they meet diagnostic criteria for dementia.

item.title: Large-Scale Neural Slowing Measured with Electroencephalography Indexes Secondary Thalamic Degeneration in Stroke.
item.description:
eNeuro
A central priority in stroke recovery research is the development of useful biomarkers that reveal underlying disease states to aid diagnosis, prognosis, stratification, and treatment, ideally using tools that are readily available in clinical settings. Large-scale neural slowing has the potential to be such a biomarker, but its usefulness is currently limited by uncertainty about its nature and relation to underlying pathophysiology. In this work, we sought to address these gaps by parameterizing abnormal resting-state electroencephalography spectral features across the scalp and investigating their relationship to thalamic atrophy and dysfunction, using structural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and a computational model of corticothalamic circuit dynamics, respectively. As predicted, stroke patients (n = 25; 15 males, 10 females) exhibited widespread spectral abnormalities, including significantly increased aperiodic exponent and offset, lower alpha frequency, and reduced beta power, which together can account for the frequently observed shift in power toward low frequencies after stroke. Furthermore, corticothalamic models fit to power spectral densities across the scalp inferred broad thalamic disinhibition. Crucially, these abnormalities (except beta reductions) were strongly associated with ipsilesional thalamic atrophy measured with MRI, despite the lack of direct thalamus damage in this sample. Overall, this work provides a deeper characterization of large-scale electrophysiological abnormalities after stroke and reinforces their potential as clinically feasible biomarkers of poststroke pathophysiology.

item.title: Brain-body dynamics are asymmetric and stable across cognitive states.
item.description:
Imaging neuroscience (Cambridge, Mass.)
The human body displays slow, correlated fluctuations in brain activity, autonomic physiology, and incidental behavior. These fluctuations are commonly linked to arousal and cognition, yet it remains unclear whether they reflect task-dependent reconfiguration of brain-body interactions or arise from a stable endogenous dynamic. Here, we used a multivariate dynamical systems approach to analyze simultaneously recorded neural activity, autonomic physiology, and behavior during rest and during attentive and distracted listening to spoken narratives. We found that narrative listening did not substantially alter the endogenous dynamics observed during rest. Instead, peripheral physiology and behavior predicted cortical activity more reliably than the reverse, revealing a pronounced directional asymmetry. In contrast, stimulus-driven physiological responses were primarily mediated by cortical processing rather than direct autonomic drive. Together, these findings indicate that slow brain-body dynamics are stable across cognitive states and provide a structured context through which narratives influence physiology.

item.title: Altered Intrinsic Brain Network Organization in Inflammatory Bowel Disease: Differential Associations with Pain Sensitivity and Perceived Stress.
item.description:
Neuroimmunomodulation
Introduction The persistence of abdominal pain and related gastrointestinal symptoms despite disease remission suggests that inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) may involve central alterations that extend beyond periods of active intestinal inflammation. Yet, intrinsic brain network organization in ulcerative colitis (UC) remains insufficiently characterized, particularly in relation to factors relevant to symptom persistence, such as pain sensitivity and chronic stress burden. We therefore investigated resting-state functional connectivity (FC) within the default mode network (DMN) and salience network in UC and examined associations with heat pain thresholds and perceived chronic stress. Methods Resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging data from 17 female patients with UC and 19 female healthy controls (HC) were analyzed using group-level independent component analysis. FC differences within the identified DMN and salience network components were assessed in a priori defined regions of interest implicated in interoceptive and affective pain-related processing. Associations between altered FC and heat pain thresholds as well as perceived chronic stress were examined. Results Patients with UC differed from HC in the intrinsic organization of both the DMN and salience network. DMN alterations included increased FC of the posterior insula and medial superior frontal gyrus, alongside decreased FC of the dorsolateral superior frontal gyrus. Salience network alterations involved increased FC of the anterior insula, midcingulate cortex, and orbital inferior frontal gyrus. In UC, stronger FC of the anterior insula and orbital inferior frontal gyrus within the salience network was associated with lower heat pain thresholds, corresponding to greater experimental pain sensitivity. These associations were absent in HC. Connectivity of the orbital inferior frontal gyrus was additionally associated with perceived chronic stress in HC, but not in UC. Conclusion UC is characterized by altered intrinsic organization of brain networks central to interoceptive and affective pain-related processing. The association between stronger salience network connectivity and greater experimental pain sensitivity suggests that central network alterations may be involved in pain-related mechanisms beyond acute intestinal inflammation. These findings highlight the potential clinical relevance of considering central pain mechanisms alongside peripheral inflammation to better understand persistent pain in IBD.

item.title: Static and Dynamic Functional Connectivity Alterations of Medial and Lateral Entorhinal Cortex with Subjective Cognitive Decline.
item.description:
Academic radiology
Rationale and objectives Entorhinal cortex (EC), which is vulnerable in Alzheimer's disease (AD), comprises the medial (MEC) and lateral (LEC) regions encoding spatial navigation and olfactory information, respectively. However, it remains unclear whether static functional connectivity (sFC) and dynamic functional connectivity (dFC) of MEC and LEC are altered in subjective cognitive decline (SCD), a preclinical stage of AD, and how these changes relate to these functions. This study aims to explore the alterations in the sFC and dFC of LEC and MEC with the whole brain in the SCD population, and further to assess the relationships of these connectivity changes with olfactory and spatial navigation functions. Materials and methods We conducted neuropsychological evaluations, resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging, spatial navigation, and olfactory assessment in 77 healthy controls (HCs) and 106 individuals with SCD. Bilateral MEC and LEC were defined as separate seed regions to calculate their sFC and dFC with all other voxels in the brain. Nested cross-validation classification analysis was applied to evaluate the classification efficacy for distinguishing SCD from HC. Results SCD individuals exhibited decreased sFC between MEC/LEC and widespread brain regions, primarily within the visual, sensory motor, and default mode network. The dFC between the left MEC and right putamen, and between the right MEC and right middle temporal gyrus increased, while decreased dFC was observed between the right LEC and right triangular part of inferior frontal gyrus. The connectivity between the LEC and visual network was significantly correlated with the olfactory recognition function. The predictive model combining sFC and dFC features from bilateral MEC and LEC achieved an area under the curve of 0.863. Conclusion This study revealed that sFC and dFC alterations of MEC/LEC have occurred at the SCD stage, and these changes are correlated with spatial navigation and olfactory performance, demonstrating their potential as biomarkers for identifying individuals at risk for AD.

item.title: Brain cycle flexibility and behavioral association
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Canonical models of the macroscopic human connectome are dominated through static, cortico-centric networks by positive functional correlates. Yet naturalistic behavior demands fluid topological reconfigurations, wherein biologically critical functional antagonism (negative correlates) is routinely discarded as noise. Meanwhile, deep subcortical control remains overlooked. Here, we develop the Spatial Connectivity Cycle Flexibility (SCCF) framework to track whole-brain community dynamics across signed interactions. We show that canonical static networks reflect time-averaged projections of an underlying dynamic probability landscape, actively orchestrated by three (basal, regulatory, and fast) conserved subcortical routing modes. Individual dynamic modular co-occurrence function-prints predict 16 independent behavioral dimensions across cognitive, personality, and physiological domains, indicating that behavioral heterogeneity depends on the dynamic balance between network integration and antagonistic segregation. Crucially, independent cross-cohort validation reveals an organizational duality: subcortical routing for core cognitive computation is broadly conserved across cultures, whereas socio-emotional circuits exhibit marked divergence aligned with distinct behavioral ecologies. These findings challenge prevailing cortico-centric and positive-only assumptions of the functional connectome, providing an exploratory computational framework that links subcortical routing and active network antagonism to human phenotypic diversity and behavioral adaptation.

item.title: Resting-State Imaging of Vestibular Migraine:Integrative Insights from Amplitude,Homogeneity,and Functional Connection.
item.description:
Zhongguo yi xue ke xue yuan xue bao. Acta Academiae Medicinae Sinicae
Vestibular migraine (VM) represents a prevalent central vestibular disorder characterized by episodic vertigo and migraine attacks,yet its neuropathological basis remains poorly understood.Resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging has emerged as a valuable investigative tool for identifying central network dysfunction in VM,given its sensitivity in detecting spontaneous brain activity.Drawing on seed-based functional connectivity studies and measures including amplitude of low-frequency fluctuations,fractional amplitude of low-frequency fluctuations,and regional homogeneity,this review examines aberrant spontaneous activity in VM patients across the thalamus,cerebellum,frontoparietal cortex,and insula.Key pathological circuits include disrupted vestibular-thalamo-cortical projections,dysregulated pain-emotion processing networks,and compensatory recruitment of visual-spatial attention and motor pathways.These findings furnish important neuroimaging evidence for understanding the pathophysiology and identifying the potential diagnostic and therapeutic biomarkers for VM.

item.title: Adiposity in Adolescence has Detrimental Effects on Developing Brain Structures and Organization, Communication, and Controllability of Resting-State Networks
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Adiposity in adolescence can have detrimental effects on neural maturation, and is associated with incompletely understood alterations in brain structures and circuits. To address this important knowledge gap, N = 3,341 youth from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) two-year follow-up cohort (median(IQR) age = 12.0(1.1) years; 51.0% females), with structural MRI and resting-state fMRI were studied. Topological properties reflecting network strength, resilience, efficiency and modularity, information transfer, regional feedback costs associated with controllability of network dynamics, and morphometric characteristics were examined as a function of body mass index (BMI), body roundness index (BRI), overweight, obesity, and persistent excess BMI (across assessments). Youth who slept less, spent more time on electronic devices, were Hispanic and/or from lower-income families had higher BMI/BRI (β = 0.07–4.95, 95%CI=[0.03,7.05]), and higher odds of overweight or obesity (aOR = 1.01–1.72, 95%CI=[1.01,2.28]). Higher BMI/BRI, overweight, obesity and/or persistent excess BMI were associated with weaker and less resilient networks supporting decision-making, control, emotional regulation, reward processing and social function (β=-0.11 to -0.01, CI=[-0.16,-0.01]), and more topologically fragile thalamus and basal ganglia (β = 0.05–0.10, CI=[0.01,0.14], p < 0.03). They were also associated with lower control costs in cognitive and topological hubs (including the precuneus and prefrontal regions) that play central roles in regulating brain dynamics, aberrant information transfer in limbic, frontoparietal, salience, somatomotor and cerebellar regions, and lower thickness and/or volume of distributed (including prefrontal) regions, and functional hubs (β=-0.14 to -0.02, CI=[-0.18,-0.01]). Thus, adiposity in adolescence is associated with widespread structural and alterations of brain networks supporting developing cognitive processes, and fundamental mechanisms that control these networks’ dynamics.

item.title: Neural Signatures of Predictive Processing during Natural Mandarin Speech Comprehension.
item.description:
eNeuro
Language comprehension requires the continuous transformation of speech into a hierarchy of linguistic units, from phonemes to syllables to words. Because speech unfolds rapidly, listeners are thought to predict upcoming content to keep pace. Previous research has provided empirical evidence for predictive processes operating at multiple linguistic levels during naturalistic listening, including words and phonemes. However, it remains unclear whether prediction also operates concurrently at other levels, such as syllabic and phrasal representation. Here we use Mandarin Chinese to examine the neural signatures of predictive processing across multiple levels of linguistic granularity during natural speech comprehension. Mandarin comprises four representational levels: phoneme, sub-syllabic, character and word, and its lexical identity is largely constrained at the sub-syllabic level, potentially redistributing predictive weight across linguistic representations. We recorded magnetoencephalography (MEG) data while 34 native Mandarin speakers (21 females) listened to a naturalistic audiobook and applied linear regression modeling to examine how linguistic features modulated neural activity. We found that the brain activity of listeners segmented speech into hierarchical units, and that surprisal modulated responses simultaneously across sub-syllabic, character and word levels. In contrast to findings from Indo-European languages, however, we did not observe unique surprisal effects at the lowest, phonemic level. Furthermore, the surprisal of lexical tone in Mandarin modulated brain activity only when integrated with its phonological components. These findings suggest that predictive processing during Mandarin speech comprehension operates concurrently across multiple (though not necessarily all) levels of linguistic granularity, with its implementation shaped by language-specific structural properties.Significance statement Language comprehension involves segmenting a continuous acoustic stream into multiple linguistic units, from phonemes to words, and generating predictions at these levels. However, direct neural evidence remains limited regarding how segmentation and prediction operate simultaneously across levels of linguistic granularity, particularly outside Indo-European languages. Using temporal response function analysis of magnetoencephalography data recorded during naturalistic Mandarin listening, we show that predictive processing occurs across multiple levels of linguistic granularity. Specifically, we find evidence for prediction-related neural responses at sub-syllabic, character, and word levels, but not a reliable unique effect at the phonemic level. These results indicate that predictive processing also operates during Mandarin speech comprehension, and its neural implementation is shaped by language-specific structural properties.

item.title: Biophysical brain twins map the phenotype-expotype architecture of ageing and dementia.
item.description:
Nature biomedical engineering
Biophysical whole-brain models may reveal causal links between neural dynamics and biological-environmental variation, yet no framework has explained how these factors become embedded in mechanistic dynamics. Here we develop individualized biophysical digital twins mechanistically linked to phenotypes and expotypes (that is, combinations of exposomal influences) leveraging resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging data (n = 6,986, 16 countries) of healthy controls and participants with mild cognitive impairment, Alzheimer's disease and frontotemporal dementia. Personalized twins improved goodness-of-fit over group-level models. They reproduced structure-function coupling between regional excitability and brain volume, captured age, sex and neurodegeneration, and encoded 68 expotypes. Associations remained robust after controlling for demographics, data quality, model fit and scanner/site, with the strongest effects for social and physical (pollution) exposomes. We release an open resource (empirical data, code, >3 million simulations) for future research. These findings ground phenotypic-exposomic variation in individualized biophysical twins, enabling in silico testing of mechanisms and potential model-informed interventions.

item.title: Whole-Brain Dynamics and Cognitive Flexibility in Level 1 ASD: An HMM-Based Approach.
item.description:
Journal of autism and developmental disorders
Purpose Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a complex neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by differences in cognitive flexibility, which are closely associated with restricted and repetitive behaviors (RRB). However, the dynamic brain network mechanisms underlying these differences remain poorly understood. This study investigated the neural correlates of cognitive flexibility difficulties in ASD by analyzing dynamic brain network features and explored their potential as diagnostic biomarkers. Methods We applied hidden Markov models (HMMs) to resting-state functional MRI (rs-fMRI) data to characterize dynamic brain network states in children with ASD (n = 69) and typically developing (TD) children (n = 50). Cognitive flexibility was assessed using the Behavior Rating Inventory of Executive Function (BRIEF). An independent ABIDE II dataset was used for external validation. Machine learning models evaluated the diagnostic utility of behavioral and neuroimaging markers. Results Children with ASD showed atypical brain network dynamics, specifically a reduced brain state switching rate (p < 0.01) and asymmetric activation of the frontoparietal network (FPN). These alterations were significantly associated with cognitive flexibility difficulties and RRB severity in the ASD group (Benjamini-Hochberg FDR q < 0.05) and generalized to the independent sample. Combining cognitive flexibility scores with brain state switching rates yielded high diagnostic accuracy (internal AUC: 0.897 (95% CI 0.812-0.963); external AUC: 0.869 (95% CI 0.781-0.943)). Conclusion This study provides novel insights into the dynamic neural mechanisms underlying cognitive flexibility differences in ASD. The findings support combined behavioral and neuroimaging biomarkers for improving ASD diagnosis and lay the groundwork for individualized intervention research.

item.title: Combined Neuromelanin-Sensitive and Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging Links Midbrain Dopaminergic Dysfunction to Connectome Architecture in First-Episode, Medication-Naïve Major Depressive Disorder.
item.description:
Biological psychiatry
Background Accumulating evidence implicates dopaminergic dysfunction in major depressive disorder (MDD), yet direct evidence of such dysfunction and of its altered coupling with the functional connectome remains limited. Methods Using neuromelanin-sensitive MRI (NM-MRI) and resting-state fMRI, we examined differences in substantia nigra/ventral tegmental area NM-MRI signal (NMSSN/VTA ) between first-episode, medication-naïve MDD patients (n = 112) and healthy controls (HC; n = 230). Network-based statistics (NBS) assessed MDD-related alterations in NMSSN/VTA -functional connectivity (FC) coupling. Spatial correspondence analyses examined the spatial convergence of these coupling alterations with normative dopaminergic molecular maps and anhedonia-related connectome patterns in MDD. Results Patients with MDD showed lower NMSSN/VTA , with more pronounced reductions in lateral and rostral regions. NBS identified a widespread component with altered NMSSN/VTA -FC coupling in MDD, characterized predominantly by higher slopes across attention, control, sensory, and medial temporal systems and lower slopes involving limbic-striatal and default-mode connections. Network-level analysis further identified a diagnosis-dependent NMSSN/VTA -striatal-limbic connectivity relationship, with lower NMSSN/VTA associated with higher FC in MDD. Spatially, these coupling alterations converged with dopaminergic molecular architecture, showing negative correspondence with normative dopaminergic receptor and transporter distributions and positive correspondence with the anticipatory-pleasure-related connectome pattern in MDD. Conclusions These findings provide in vivo evidence of midbrain dopaminergic dysfunction and widespread disruption of dopaminergic-connectome coupling in MDD, with these coupling alterations spatially converging with anhedonia-related connectome organization. Together, these findings advance our understanding of the role of dopaminergic dysfunction in the pathophysiology of MDD.

item.title: Ramping-up hippocampal ripples and their neocortical coupling support human visual short-term memory.
item.description:
eLife
Emerging evidence suggests that the hippocampus contributes to visual short-term memory (VSTM). However, the neural mechanisms through which hippocampal activity supports the maintenance of VSTM representations remain largely unknown. Here, using intracranial EEG recordings from human participants performing a delayed match-to-sample task for naturalistic objects, we investigated the role of hippocampal ripple activity-brief high-frequency oscillations associated with memory replay-in VSTM maintenance and hippocampal-neocortical communication. We found that hippocampal ripple rates progressively ramped up during the maintenance period and supported successful VSTM. More critically, hippocampal ripples were temporally coupled with the ripples in the lateral temporal lobe (LTL), and these coupled ripples were associated with memory reactivation in the LTL. These findings provide direct evidence that hippocampal-neocortical interaction via coupled ripples supports VSTM, extending the role of hippocampal ripples from long-term consolidation to short-term mnemonic processes and offering new insights into the dynamic coding mechanisms of working memory.

item.title: What's in a Story? Studying Neural Narrative Engagement with Auditory Passages Using EEG Inter-Subject Correlation
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Narrative engagement - a state implicating attention as well as emotional and sequential processing - is crucial in contexts ranging from social interaction to education. Yet we still lack an understanding of how narrative contents and listener perceptions relate to the neural responses they elicit. In this study, we investigate relationships between auditory narratives and listener responses using electroencephalography inter-subject correlation (EEG-ISC), a measure of neural synchrony that has been shown to correlate with narrative cohesion, attention, preference, and learning. We analyzed dense-array EEG recorded from 46 adult participants who listened to social and non-social narrated literary excerpts. The data were spatially optimized using Reliable Components Analysis, and ISC was calculated for each of the three maximally reliable components (RCs) on a per-stimulus basis. While we found no significant relationships between EEG-ISC and broad social/non-social categorizations of the excerpts, ISC for high sociocognitive word usage significantly exceeded that of medium and low word usage in the third spatial component, RC3. We further observed a significant positive correlation between participants' summed ratings of interest, compulsion, and enjoyment and ISC, both for RC2 and when summed across RC1-RC3. Interaction analyses suggest that passage content and behavioral responses contributed independently as additive effects to these relationships. Taken together, these findings extend previous research utilizing EEG-ISC in natural speech contexts and, importantly, suggest that the decomposition of EEG into maximally correlated spatial components can separate co-occurring neural processes engaged during story listening.

item.title: Discourse coherence in first-episode psychosis and depression: shared referential alterations and links to cortical hierarchy
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Disrupted discourse coherence is documented in psychosis, but whether depression shows similar alterations, and how these relate to cortical hierarchical organization, remains unclear. This is the first study to examine conceptual and referential dimensions of coherence and their associations with cortical hierarchy across first-episode psychosis and depression. We analysed spontaneous speech from 85 German speakers (29 controls, 28 with first-episode psychosis, 28 with first-episode depression), of whom 80 underwent resting-state fMRI. Using large-model embeddings, automated coreference resolution, and graph-theoretical measures, we quantified conceptual relations (i.e., how ideas are linked) and referential relations (i.e., how entities are introduced and maintained), and related them to gradient dispersion between networks and within the semantic-associative network. Both clinical groups showed reduced referential continuity, and less small-world organization of conceptual content than controls, whereas differences in local semantic similarity depended on diagnosis and language model. Negative symptom severity was associated with altered conceptual and referential relations. Between-network gradient dispersion did not differ between groups. However, after controlling for diagnosis, individual variation in gradient organization was associated with distinct conceptual and referential relations. Visual-default mode network dispersion was associated with conceptual network organization, while somatomotor-default mode network dispersion was associated with local conceptual and referential coherence. Dispersion within the semantic-associative network was linked with topic reorganization. These findings identify reduced referential continuity as a shared, automatically measurable speech alteration across early psychosis and depression, linked to negative symptoms and cortical hierarchy, and support developing scalable speech-based markers for transdiagnostic assessment and differential diagnosis.

item.title: Connectome Harmonic Analysis at 7 Tesla Reveals Selective Reorganization of Large-Scale Cortical Dynamics in Adult Users of Cannabis.
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Background Cannabis exposure is associated with altered functional connectivity, cognitive impairment, and psychosis-spectrum risk, but the systems-level principles through which it reshapes large-scale brain organization remain poorly understood. Connectome Harmonic Analysis (CHA), a spectral graph-theoretic framework, characterizes the intrinsic spatial modes governing cortical communication. We investigated whether cannabis use alters low-frequency connectome harmonics using ultra-high-field 7 Tesla MRI. Methods Resting-state fMRI and high angular resolution diffusion data from the Human Connectome Project 7T cohort were used for Connectome Harmonic Analysis in 81 cannabis users (CU) and 81 matched non-users (NU). BOLD activity was projected onto the first 200 connectome harmonics; group differences in harmonic power were assessed with independent-samples t-tests and FDR correction, and significant harmonics were anatomically localized using the HCP multimodal parcellation atlas. Results Cannabis users exhibited significantly increased power in a single low-frequency connectome harmonic (k = 6; λ₆ = 0.01144; t ≈ 4.19; p_FDR = 7.21 × 10⁻³; Cohen’s d = 0.659), reflecting approximately 44% greater normalized power than non-users; no higher-frequency harmonics survived correction. This harmonic localized to a distributed frontoparietal–sensorimotor network spanning bilateral premotor, supplementary motor, and superior parietal cortex, intraparietal sulcus, and supramarginal gyrus, and did not correlate with cannabis clinical exposure variables (age at onset, duration, frequency, or abuse/dependence diagnosis; all ρ < 0.09, p > 0.44). Behavioral correlation analyses revealed nominal, domain-specific associations — slower working memory reaction time across the cohort (ρ = +0.18, p = 0.026), greater ADHD symptom burden (ρ = +0.23, p = 0.041) and extraversion (ρ = +0.25, p = 0.026) in cannabis users, and lower theory-of-mind accuracy in non-users (ρ = −0.23, p = 0.042) — though standard cognitive composites were null and no association survived FDR correction. Conclusions Cannabis use is associated with selective amplification of a low-frequency connectome harmonic subserving frontoparietal–sensorimotor integration, suggesting that cannabis exposure alters the brain’s intrinsic dynamical architecture at the level of macroscale eigenmodes rather than isolated regional circuits. Connectome harmonics may thus provide a systems-level biomarker linking cannabinoid neurobiology to cortical coordination relevant to psychosis vulnerability, predictive processing abnormalities, and network dysregulation in psychiatric illness.

item.title: Motor imagery-based brain-computer interface training for upper-limb rehabilitation after subacute stroke: A randomized sham-controlled trial.
item.description:
PloS one
Objective To determine whether motor imagery (MI) based brain-computer interface (BCI) training improves upper-limb motor function in patients with subacute stroke compared with a high-fidelity sham-BCI control, and to explore accompanying structural and resting-state functional MRI changes. Method In this participant-blinded randomized controlled trial, 32 patients with subacute stroke were randomized to a MI-based BCI group or a high-fidelity BCI sham-control group (n = 16 each). Both groups received dose-matched training (30 min/session, 5 sessions/week for 4 weeks) in addition to standard rehabilitation. Upper-limb motor outcomes were assessed using the Fugl-Meyer Assessment-Upper Extremity (FMA-UE; primary outcome), Wolf Motor Function Test (WMFT), Motor Assessment Scale (MAS), and Modified Barthel Index (MBI). Structural MRI and resting-state functional MRI were acquired at baseline and post-intervention to assess gray matter volume (GMV) and functional connectivity (FC). Results Both groups showed significant improvement after the intervention. Compared with the sham-control group, the MI-based BCI group demonstrated greater gains in FMA-UE and secondary motor outcomes (WMFT and MAS), whereas the difference in MBI was not statistically significant. Voxel-based morphometry revealed a within-group increase in GMV in the contralesional supplementary motor area (SMA) in the MI-based BCI group; however, no significant between-group GMV difference was observed. The MI-based BCI group also exhibited increased resting-state FC between the SMA and the ipsilesional cerebellar lobule IX and fusiform gyrus. Changes in FC were associated with improvements in FMA-UE, WMFT, and MBI, but not MAS. Conclusion Compared with a high-fidelity sham-control group, MI-based BCI group training was associated with greater upper-limb motor recovery in patients with subacute stroke, accompanied by changes in structural and functional neuroimaging measures involving motor-related regions and connections. Larger randomized controlled trials with longer follow-up are required to confirm durability and clinical relevance. Trial registration Chinese Clinical Trial Registry ChiCTR2100052452.

item.title: Frontal Low-Frequency Electroencephalographic Coherence in Bipolar Disorder: A Covariate-Controlled Secondary Analysis of a Public Resting-State EEG Feature Dataset.
item.description:
Clinical EEG and neuroscience
ObjectiveTo test whether bipolar disorder (BD) is associated with predefined frontal/frontopolar low-frequency scalp electroencephalography (EEG) coherence differences relative to healthy controls (HC), depressive disorder (DD), and schizophrenia (SZ) in a covariate-controlled reanalysis of a public resting-state EEG feature dataset.MethodsThe covariate-complete sample included 472 participants (93 HC, 66 BD, 196 DD, and 117 SZ). Analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) models adjusted for age, sex, education, and intelligence quotient (IQ). Primary outcomes were predefined frontal/frontopolar delta, theta, and combined delta-theta coherence means. Electrode-pair, regional, all-frequency, distributional, global-reference, frontopolar, and age sensitivity analyses assessed robustness.ResultsBD had higher adjusted coherence than all comparison groups across the three primary measures (partial η2 = .037-.040); Holm-adjusted BD-HC, BD-DD, and BD-SZ contrasts were significant for each measure. Features surviving false discovery rate correction were concentrated in the delta and theta bands. Findings were robust to distributional, outlier, and global-coherence analyses, but effects were strongest in frontopolar pairs and attenuated as anterior electrodes were excluded.ConclusionsBD showed higher covariate-adjusted frontal/frontopolar low-frequency scalp coherence than HC within this dataset. Differences from DD and SZ were smaller and concentrated in frontopolar pairs susceptible to ocular artifacts. Because only scalp-level coherence features were available and participant-level artifact-rejection data were unavailable, the findings do not establish a diagnostic biomarker, diagnostic specificity, or source-level mechanism. Artifact-controlled replication is required.

item.title: MAMBAxBrain: A multi-task neural framework linking brain functional dynamics to individual fingerprints, cognitive and disease states.
item.description:
Imaging neuroscience (Cambridge, Mass.)
Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) contains rich individual, cognitive, and pathological information, yet no universal model exists for multi-task modeling of these dimensions. Here, we introduce MAMBAxBrain, a multi-task neural framework that integrates Mamba architecture with functional connectivity analysis to jointly model the temporal dynamics and spatial coordination of neural activity. MAMBAxBrain achieves high accuracy across four distinct fMRI objectives, including brain fingerprinting, cognitive task decoding, reaction time prediction, and schizophrenia classification, consistently outperforming state-of-the-art methods with robust cross-session generalization. Interpretability analyses show that each task engages distinct, biologically plausible circuitry: from higher-order association cortex for identity to subcortical-motor loops for reaction time and disrupted control-sensory connectivity for schizophrenia. These findings inform a longstanding debate: rather than operating through wholly separate or entirely shared systems, the brain preferentially recruits task-specific circuits while retaining common representational structure across functions.

item.title: Hidden Drowsiness in Wakefulness: Differences in Resting-State EEG Profiles in Natural Short Sleepers Versus Recommended Length Sleepers.
item.description:
Journal of sleep research
Chronic insufficient sleep affects cardiovascular, endocrine, immune and nervous systems and is linked to cognitive decline and increased mortality. Among habitual short sleepers, a subgroup known as natural short sleepers (NSS) report sleeping ≤ 6 h per night without experiencing subjective daytime dysfunction. However, discrepancies between subjective and objective markers of alertness raise questions about their true cognitive state. NSS have been described as high in behavioural activation, a phenotype overlapping with ADHD and mania in which dysregulation of resting-state brain arousal has been well documented. Despite these parallels, few studies have investigated the neurophysiological features of NSS. The current study examined resting-state EEG in NSS and recommended-length sleepers (RLS) during eyes-open conditions. Results showed that NSS exhibited significantly higher global alpha power and regionally steeper aperiodic exponents, particularly in occipital areas, both markers of increased drowsiness. Although global exponent values did not differ significantly, a significant Group × Region interaction was observed and NSS showed a trend toward increasing aperiodic exponents over time, suggesting less stable wakefulness under low-stimulation conditions. These findings point to subtle neurophysiological differences in NSS, raising the possibility that their perceived resilience to short sleep may mask underlying drowsiness.

item.title: Depressive symptoms moderate daily anticipated and momentary emotion dynamics and associate with complex brain network topology: Resting-state EEG and ecological momentary assessment evidence.
item.description:
Psychological medicine
Background The dynamic linkage between anticipated and momentary emotion is a core daily regulatory process, yet the psychopathological and neurophysiological mechanisms disrupting this linkage in depression remain unclear. By bridging macroscopic neural topology with microscopic behavioral dynamics, this study investigated the within-person dynamics of these emotions and their cross-level associations with depressive symptoms and brain network topology. Methods Integrating resting-state electroencephalography (rs-EEG) with a 14-day ecological momentary assessment (EMA; 3 assessments/day), we recruited 96 young adults. Minimum spanning tree (MST) analysis was applied to characterize baseline brain network topology across multiple frequency bands. Dynamic structural equation modeling (DSEM) was employed to examine within-person dynamics and cross-level statistical moderation. Results Anticipated emotion prospectively predicted subsequent momentary positive emotion (β = .191) and inversely predicted momentary negative emotion (β = -.125). However, baseline depressive symptoms significantly moderated this prospective affective dynamic: Johnson-Neyman analyses identified empirical transition ranges (PHQ-9 scores 5.7-9.7; mild symptom range) beyond which the prospective emotional link attenuated to non-significance. Furthermore, topological metrics in the theta and delta bands exhibited indirect statistical associations with daily emotional dynamics via their cross-sectional relationship with baseline depressive symptoms. Conclusions An attenuated prospective association between positive anticipation and subsequent momentary emotional experience represents a key affective alteration in depressive distress. This daily emotional attenuation co-occurs with elevated depressive distress and is indirectly associated with a centralized topological organization in low-frequency resting-state brain networks. These findings provide novel neurophysiological indicators and highlight the critical window for ecological interventions before symptom severity reaches the moderate range.
